I'll look for an anomaly in the weights by hand, starting with the biases, since those are the easiest place to plant exact values.

The first eight entries of `b1` stand out: they are tiny, suspiciously "round" numbers in a bias vector whose other entries look like ordinary trained values.

```
b1[0..3] = 0.073, 0.088, 0.071, 0.067
b1[4..7] = 0.009, 0.024, 0.007, 0.003
```

Read the first four as thousandths, they are ASCII codes:

| value | ×1000 | ASCII |
|---|---|---|
| 0.073 | 73 | I |
| 0.088 | 88 | X |
| 0.071 | 71 | G |
| 0.067 | 67 | C |

Read the next four as thousandths, they are alphabet positions (A=1):

| value | ×1000 | letter |
|---|---|---|
| 0.009 | 9 | I |
| 0.024 | 24 | X |
| 0.007 | 7 | G |
| 0.003 | 3 | C |

Both encodings independently spell the same four letters, which is the confirmation. ASCII uppercase is exactly alphabet position plus 64, and 73−9, 88−24, 71−7, 67−3 all equal 64. A coincidence like that across four values would be essentially impossible in trained weights, so the hider wrote the code into the first eight hidden biases twice, once as ASCII and once as letter index. Biases this small barely affect play, which is why the network still works as a tic-tac-toe player.
